scenario: A conversation between two individuals in a new romantic relationship
learner_goal: Admit to having an affair (<extra_info>Extra information: you had an affair during your previous relationship which ended recently</extra_info>)
partner_goal: Maintain trust in the relationship (<extra_info>Extra information: you believed in complete honesty from the beginning of the relationship</extra_info>)

transcript.speaker: Sasha Ramirez
transcript.content: Ava, I need to tell you something before we go any deeper. During my last relationship I had an affair — it’s something I regret and it’s part of why that relationship ended. I’m telling you because I care about you and want to be honest from the start.

transcript.speaker: Ava Thompson
transcript.content: Thank you for telling me — I know that took courage. I believe honesty is everything, and I really appreciate you trusting me with this. Can you tell me when this happened and whether it’s entirely in the past or something you’re still worried about? I want to be supportive, and I also need clarity so we can keep building trust.

transcript.speaker: Sasha Ramirez
transcript.content: It happened about a year before we split up. It’s entirely in the past—I’m not in contact with that person and it’s one of the reasons that relationship ended. I regret it deeply and I’ve been working through why I did it (therapy and a lot of reflection). I want to be honest with you and earn your trust, so ask me anything you need to know.

transcript.speaker: Ava Thompson
transcript.content: Thank you again for being so honest, Sasha. I believe you, and I’m really glad you told me—and that you’ve been doing the work in therapy. That gives me a lot of comfort. I don’t want to dwell on the past, but could you share what you learned from it and what concrete steps you’re taking to make sure it won’t happen again? Are there any triggers or situations I should know about so I can support you? I care about you and want us to keep being open—I may need reassurance sometimes, and I hope that’s okay.

transcript.speaker: Sasha Ramirez
transcript.content: I learned that loneliness and poor communication became excuses for selfish choices, and I take full responsibility for that. Since then I’m in regular therapy, I cut all contact and deleted their number, I changed my routines, and I check in with a close friend and my therapist when stress or temptation feels strong. If you need reassurance, tell me what helps — I’m committed to transparency, open check-ins, and even couples therapy if that would help me earn your trust.

transcript.speaker: Ava Thompson
transcript.content: Thank you — that really means a lot. I believe you, and I’m glad you’ve been doing the work to understand what happened. What would help me feel secure are a few concrete things: regular check-ins when one of us is stressed or distant, a quick heads-up if you’re feeling tempted or overwhelmed (even just “I’m struggling today”), and continuing to lean on your therapist and friend like you already do. I’m open to couples therapy down the line if we want extra support. I trust you, Sasha, and I’ll ask for reassurance sometimes — I hope that’s okay. Would you be comfortable with those things?

scenario_title: Sensitive honesty in a new romantic relationship, high vulnerability and risk of rejection | skills from the partner disclosing past infidelity navigating truthful admission while preserving emerging trust
social_dynamic: Sensitive honesty in a new romantic relationship, high vulnerability and risk of rejection
